per_question.user_input: Can I deduct mortgage interest on my primary home?
per_question.response:
Yes, you can generally deduct mortgage interest on your primary home, but several conditions must be met:

**Basic Requirements:**
- You must file Form 1040 or 1040-SR and **itemize deductions on Schedule A** (Form 1040) [Pub 936, p.2].
- The mortgage must be a **secured debt** on a **qualified home** in which you have an ownership interest [Pub 936, p.2].
- Both you and the lender must intend that the loan be repaid [Pub 936, p.2].

**What Counts as a Qualified Home:**
Your primary home (main home) qualifies. A home includes a house, condominium, cooperative, mobile home, house trailer, boat, or similar property that has sleeping, cooking, and toilet facilities [Pub 936, p.4].

**Loan Limits:**
- You can deduct home mortgage interest on the first **$750,000** ($375,000 if married filing separately) of indebtedness for mortgages taken out after December 16, 2017 [Pub 936, p.1].
- Higher limits of **$1,000,000** ($500,000 if married filing separately) apply if the indebtedness was incurred before December 16, 2017 [Pub 936, p.1].

**Fully Deductible Interest:**
In most cases, you can deduct **all** of your home mortgage interest if your mortgage balances fall within the limits above and the mortgage was used to buy, build, or substantially improve your home [Pub 936, pp.2–3].

**Important Notes:**
- **Home equity loan/line of credit interest** is deductible *only* if the borrowed funds were used to buy, build, or substantially improve the home securing the loan [Pub 936, pp.1–2].
- **Mortgage insurance premiums** are no longer deductible — that itemized deduction has expired [Pub 936, p.1].

In summary, if you itemize deductions, have a secured mortgage on your main home, and your loan balance is within the applicable limits, your mortgage interest is deductible.

per_question.user_input: What is the standard deduction for a single filer in 2024?
per_question.response:
Based on the IRS publication excerpts provided, the figures cited relate to **2025** tax year amounts, not 2024. However, one excerpt does reference the 2024 standard deduction indirectly.

For **2025**, the standard deduction for a **single filer** is **$15,750** [Pub 17, p.3], [Pub 501, pp.25-26], [Pub 17, p.97].

For **2024**, the standard deduction for a single filer (filing jointly) is referenced indirectly in an example: "The standard deduction that you could have claimed was **$29,200**" for a *joint* return [Pub 525, pp.25-26], which implies the 2024 single filer standard deduction would be $14,600 (half of $29,200), but this figure is not explicitly stated in the provided excerpts.

> ⚠️ **Note:** The provided IRS publication excerpts do not explicitly state the 2024 standard deduction for a single filer. The excerpts focus primarily on **2025** tax year figures. If you need the confirmed 2024 amount, please refer directly to IRS Publication 501 (2024) or the 2024 Form 1040 instructions.

per_question.user_input: Are contributions to a traditional IRA tax deductible?
per_question.response:
Yes, contributions to a traditional IRA **may** be tax deductible, but the deductibility depends on several factors. Here is a detailed breakdown:

---

### General Rule
You may be able to deduct some or all of your contributions to a traditional IRA, depending on your circumstances [Pub 590-A, p.6]. Specifically, you can generally deduct the **lesser of**:
- The contributions to your traditional IRA for the year, **or**
- The general limit (or the Kay Bailey Hutchison Spousal IRA limit, if applicable) [Pub 590-A, pp.11]

---

### Contribution Limits (2025)
For 2025, the general deductible contribution limit is:
- **$7,000**, or
- **$8,000** if you were age 50 or older by the end of 2025 [Pub 17, pp.81-82]

---

### Full Deduction
If **neither you nor your spouse** was covered for any part of the year by an employer retirement plan, you can take a **full deduction** for total contributions to one or more traditional IRAs of up to the lesser of $7,000 ($8,000 if age 50 or older) or 100% of your compensation [Pub 17, pp.81-82].

---

### Possible Limitations
Deductibility may be **reduced or eliminated** based on:
1. **Employer retirement plan coverage**: If you or your spouse were covered by an employer retirement plan during the year, you may not be able to deduct the full amount [Pub 590-A, p.11].
2. **Income and filing status**: Deductibility depends on your income, filing status, whether you are covered by a retirement plan at work, and whether you receive Social Security benefits [Pub 590-A, p.5].

---

### Other Notes
- **Trustees' administrative fees** billed separately are **not** deductible as IRA contributions or as itemized deductions [Pub 590-A, p.11].
- **Brokers' commissions** are considered part of your IRA contribution and are deductible subject to the limits [Pub 17, pp.81-82].

per_question.user_input: How long must I hold a stock to qualify for long-term capital gains rates?
per_question.response:
To qualify for **long-term capital gains rates**, you must hold a stock for **more than 1 year** (i.e., longer than 12 months) [p550, p.81].

Here are the key details:

- **Long-term**: If you hold investment property **more than 1 year**, any capital gain or loss is treated as a long-term capital gain or loss, qualifying for the preferential long-term capital gains tax rates [p550, p.81].
- **Short-term**: If you hold the property **1 year or less**, any capital gain or loss is short-term and taxed at ordinary income rates [p550, p.81].

**How to count your holding period:**
- Start counting on the **day after** the day you acquired the property.
- The **day you disposed of the property** (sold it) counts as part of your holding period [p550, p.81].

> **Example:** If you bought stock on January 31, 2024, you would need to sell it on or after February 1, 2025, for the gain to be considered long-term [p550, p.81].

**Note for mutual fund or REIT stock:** Special rules may apply if you hold such stock for 6 months or less and sell it at a loss — a portion of that loss may be recharacterized as long-term [p550, pp.82-83].

Also note that **qualified dividends** have a separate, different holding period requirement: you must have held the stock for more than 60 days during the 121-day period beginning 60 days before the ex-dividend date to qualify for the favorable 0%, 15%, or 20% tax rate on those dividends [p550, p.28].

per_question.user_input: Is money received as a gift taxable income to the recipient?
per_question.response:
In most cases, **money or property received as a gift is NOT taxable income to the recipient**. However, there are important nuances to be aware of:

1. **Gifts are generally excluded from income.** "In most cases, property you receive as a gift, bequest, or inheritance isn't included in your income." [Pub 525, p.33] [Pub 17, p.78]

2. **Income later produced by gifted property IS taxable.** "However, if property you receive this way later produces income such as interest, dividends, or rents, that income is taxable to you." [Pub 525, p.33] [Pub 17, p.78]

3. **Trust income is taxable.** "If property is given to a trust and the income from it is paid, credited, or distributed to you, that income is also taxable to you." [Pub 525, p.33] [Pub 17, p.78]

4. **If the gift itself IS the income from property, it's taxable.** "If the gift, bequest, or inheritance is the income from the property, that income is taxable to you." [Pub 525, p.33] [Pub 17, p.78]

5. **Virtual currency received as a gift has special rules.** "If you receive virtual currency as a bona fide gift, you will not recognize income until you sell, exchange, or otherwise dispose of that virtual currency." [Pub 550, p.60]

6. **Inherited pensions or IRAs may be partially taxable.** "If you inherited a pension or an IRA, you may have to include part of the inherited amount in your income." [Pub 525, p.33]

**Summary:** The gift itself is generally not taxable to the recipient. However, any income that the gifted property subsequently generates (e.g., interest, dividends, rent) is taxable to the recipient.

per_question.user_input: What filing status can a single parent use if they paid more than half the cost of keeping a home for a qualifying child?
per_question.response:
A single parent who paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home for a qualifying child can use the **Head of Household** filing status.

Specifically, to qualify for head of household, you must meet all of the following requirements [Pub 501, p.8]:

1. You are **unmarried or considered unmarried** on the last day of the year.
2. You **paid more than half the cost of keeping up a home** for the year.
3. A **qualifying person lived with you in the home for more than half the year** (except for temporary absences, such as school).

As an added benefit, if you qualify to file as head of household, your **tax rate will usually be lower** than the rates for single or married filing separately, and you will also receive a **higher standard deduction** than if you file as single or married filing separately [Pub 501, p.8].

To select this filing status, check the "Head of household" box on the Filing Status line near the top of Form 1040 or 1040-SR. If the child who qualifies you for this filing status isn't claimed as your dependent in the Dependents section of Form 1040 or 1040-SR, enter the child's name in the entry space below the filing status checkboxes [Pub 501, p.8].

per_question.user_input: What is the penalty for filing a federal tax return late when tax is owed?
per_question.response:
When you file a federal tax return late and owe tax, several penalties may apply:

## Failure-to-File Penalty
- The standard penalty is **5% of the unpaid tax for each month or part of a month** that the return is late, up to a maximum of **25%** [p17, pp.21-22].
- If the failure to file is due to **fraud**, the penalty increases to **15% per month**, up to a maximum of **75%** [p17, pp.21-22].
- If your return is **more than 60 days late**, the minimum penalty is the **smaller of $525 or 100% of the unpaid tax** [p17, pp.21-22].
- **Exception:** You won't owe the penalty if you can show the failure to file was due to **reasonable cause and not willful neglect** [p17, pp.21-22].

## Failure-to-Pay Penalty
- You must also pay a **failure-to-pay penalty of 0.50% (½ of 1%) of your unpaid taxes for each month**, or part of a month, after the due date that the tax isn't paid [p17, p.22].
- This penalty is **reduced to 0.25% per month** if an installment agreement is in effect for that month (and you filed your return by the due date, including extensions) [p17, p.22].
- If a **notice of intent to levy** is issued, the rate increases to **1%** at the start of the first month beginning at least 10 days after the notice is issued [p17, p.22].
- If a **notice and demand for immediate payment** is issued, the rate increases to **1%** at the start of the first month beginning after the day the notice is issued [p17, p.22].
- This penalty cannot exceed **25% of your unpaid tax** [p17, p.22].
- The failure-to-pay penalty does **not** apply during the automatic 6-month extension period if you paid at least **90% of your actual tax liability** by the original due date and pay the balance when you file [p17, p.22].

## Combined Penalties
- If both penalties apply in any month, the **5% (or 15%) failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay penalty** [p17, p.22].
- However, if your return is more than 60 days late, the minimum penalty remains the smaller of **$525 or 100% of the unpaid tax** [p17, p.22].

per_question.user_input: What is the additional standard deduction amount for a single taxpayer who is age 65 or older in 2024?
per_question.response:
Based on the provided IRS publication excerpts, the specific dollar amount of the **additional standard deduction for a single taxpayer age 65 or older for 2024** is not explicitly stated in the excerpts provided. The excerpts primarily reference **2025** figures and tables.

Here is what the excerpts do tell us:

- Taxpayers who are age 65 or older on the last day of the year and don't itemize deductions are entitled to a **higher (additional) standard deduction** [p501, p.23].
- The standard deduction for 2025 is **higher than it was for 2024** [p501, p.1].
- For 2025, the filing requirement thresholds show that a single taxpayer under 65 has a gross income threshold of **$15,750**, while a single taxpayer age 65 or older has a threshold of **$17,750** — a difference of **$2,000** — which reflects the additional standard deduction amount for age in 2025 [p501, pp.1-2].

However, the excerpts do **not directly state** the additional standard deduction amount for a single taxpayer age 65 or older for the **2024** tax year. The excerpts reference tables (e.g., Table 6, Table 7, Table 10-2) to figure the exact standard deduction amount, but those tables are not included in the provided excerpts [p501, p.23; p17, p.94].

To find the precise 2024 additional standard deduction amount for a single filer age 65 or older, you would need to consult the 2024 version of IRS Publication 501 or Publication 17 and their associated standard deduction tables.

per_question.user_input: What is the gross income limit for claiming someone as a qualifying relative dependent?
per_question.response:
For 2025, the gross income limit for claiming someone as a qualifying relative dependent is **less than $5,200**. This is known as the **Gross Income Test**, and it requires that a person's gross income for the year must be less than $5,200 in order to qualify [p501, pp.19, 36]. This threshold is confirmed across multiple IRS publications — for example, IRS Publication 503 also states that "in determining whether you may claim a person as a qualifying relative for 2025, the person's gross income must be less than $5,200" [p503, p.3].

**Key point:** Gross income includes all income in the form of money, property, and services that is not exempt from tax [p17, pp.35-36]. If the person's gross income equals or exceeds $5,200, they generally cannot be claimed as a qualifying relative dependent (though there is an exception for certain individuals who couldn't be claimed solely because their income reached $5,200 or more — for example, in the context of dependent care credits) [p503, p.3].

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct the cost of prescription eyeglasses as a medical expense?
per_question.response:
Yes, you can deduct the cost of prescription eyeglasses as a medical expense. According to IRS Publication 502, "you can include in medical expenses amounts you pay for eyeglasses and contact lenses needed for medical reasons" [p502, p.7]. This applies as long as the eyeglasses are needed for medical reasons (i.e., to correct a vision deficiency).

Additionally, related vision expenses that are also deductible include:
- **Eye exams**: "You can include in medical expenses the amount you pay for eye examinations" [p502, p.7].
- **Eye surgery**: "You can include in medical expenses the amount you pay for eye surgery to treat defective vision, such as laser eye surgery or radial keratotomy" [p502, p.7].
- **Contact lenses**: Including the cost of equipment and materials such as saline solution and enzyme cleaner needed for their use [p502, pp.6-7].

To actually claim this deduction, medical expenses must be itemized on Schedule A (Form 1040), and only the portion of total medical expenses that exceeds 7.5% of your adjusted gross income (AGI) is deductible [p502, p.2].

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct health insurance premiums I pay out of pocket as a medical expense?
per_question.response:
Yes, in most cases you **can** deduct health insurance premiums you pay out of pocket as a medical expense. Here are the key rules:

---

### ✅ What You CAN Include

- **Out-of-pocket premiums for medical care policies** — You can include insurance premiums you pay for policies that cover medical care, such as hospitalization, surgical services, X-rays, prescription drugs, dental care, and more [p502, p.8].
- **Medicare Part B and Part D premiums** — Premiums you pay for Medicare Part B (supplemental medical insurance) and Medicare Part D (prescription drug coverage) are deductible as medical expenses [p502, p.8].
- **Medicare Part A premiums** (if voluntarily enrolled) — If you aren't covered under Social Security and voluntarily enroll in Medicare Part A, you can include those premiums as a medical expense [p502, p.8].
- **HMO payments** — Amounts paid to an HMO for medical care coverage are treated as medical insurance premiums and are deductible [p502, pp.7-8].

---

### ❌ What You CANNOT Include

- **Employer-sponsored plan premiums (pre-tax)** — Don't include premiums paid by an employer-sponsored health insurance plan unless those premiums are included on your Form W-2 [p502, p.8].
- **Premiums paid through the Premium Tax Credit** — You cannot include premiums paid by or through the premium tax credit. However, any advance payments of the premium tax credit that you *had to pay back* can be included [p502, p.12; p502, p.16].
- **Premiums paid with tax-free retirement distributions** — You cannot include health or long-term care insurance premiums if you elected to pay them with tax-free distributions from a retirement plan [p502, p.9].
- **Certain types of policies** — Premiums for life insurance, loss-of-earnings policies, loss of limb/sight policies, guaranteed weekly hospital benefit policies, and the medical portion of car insurance (when not separately stated) are **not** deductible [p502, p.9].
- **Retired public safety officers** — Cannot include health or long-term care insurance premiums paid with tax-free retirement plan distributions [p502, p.8].

---

### 📝 Important Note
You cannot include premiums that were paid **and** for which you are also claiming a credit or deduction elsewhere — no double-dipping [p502, p.8].

In summary, as long as you are paying the premiums out of your own pocket (after-tax), and none of the exclusions above apply, those premiums are includible as a medical expense on Schedule A (Form 1040).

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum amount of qualifying expenses for the child and dependent care credit for one qualifying person?
per_question.response:
The maximum amount of qualifying expenses for the child and dependent care credit for **one qualifying person is $3,000**. This is a yearly dollar limit on the amount of work-related expenses you can use to figure the credit [p503, p.12]. The amount of the dollar limit remains the same no matter how long, during the year, you have a qualifying person in your household — you use the $3,000 limit if you had one qualifying person at any time during the year [p503, p.12].

Note: If you exclude or deduct dependent care benefits provided by a dependent care benefit plan, the $3,000 limit will be reduced by the amount excluded or deducted, potentially lowering the amount of expenses you can use to claim the credit [p503, pp.2-3].

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum age of a child who qualifies for the child and dependent care credit?
per_question.response:
For the **child and dependent care credit**, a qualifying child must have been **under age 13** when the care was provided. Specifically, a qualifying person for this credit includes "your qualifying child who is your dependent and who was under age 13 when the care was provided" [p503, p.3]. This is also confirmed in the introduction, which states the credit applies if you pay someone to care for "your dependent who is under age 13" [p503, pp.1-2].

**Important note:** If the child is disabled (not physically or mentally able to care for themselves) and lived with you for more than half the year, there is no age limit — they can qualify regardless of age [p503, p.3].

Also note that this age limit (under 13) is **different** from the Child Tax Credit (CTC), which requires a child to be under age 17 [p17, p.111].

per_question.user_input: Can I claim the child and dependent care credit if I pay a relative to care for my child?
per_question.response:
Yes, you **can** claim the child and dependent care credit if you pay a relative to care for your child — but only if that relative does **not** fall into certain disqualified categories. Here is a breakdown of the rules:

**You CAN pay a relative if:**
- The relative is **not** someone you (or your spouse) can claim as a dependent [Pub 503, p.2].
- The relative is **not** your spouse [Pub 503, p.2].
- The relative is **not** the parent of your qualifying child (if the child is under age 13) [Pub 503, p.2].
- If the relative is your own child, they must be **age 19 or older** by the end of the year [Pub 503, p.2].

**You CANNOT pay the following relatives and claim the credit:**
1. **Your spouse** [Pub 503, p.2].
2. **The parent** of your qualifying child, if that child is your child and is under age 13 [Pub 503, p.2].
3. **Your own child** (including stepchild or foster child) if they are **under age 19** at the end of the year [Pub 503, p.2].
4. **Any person you or your spouse can claim as a dependent** [Pub 503, p.2].

This is also illustrated in the IRS flowchart (Figure A), which confirms that payments to a spouse, the parent of a qualifying child under 13, or a child under 19 will disqualify the credit [Pub 503, p.5].

**Other requirements still apply**, regardless of who provides care. You must also:
- Have **earned income** during the year [Pub 503, p.2].
- Pay the expenses to allow you (or your spouse) to **work or look for work** [Pub 503, pp.5-6].
- Identify the care provider (name, address, and taxpayer identification number) on **Form 2441** [Pub 503, pp.2-3].

**In summary:** Paying a relative is permissible as long as that relative is not your dependent, not your spouse, not the parent of your qualifying child under 13, and not your child under age 19. If those conditions are met, you may be able to claim the credit for up to 35% of qualifying employment-related expenses [Pub 503, pp.1-2].

per_question.user_input: How does an employer-provided dependent care assistance program affect the child and dependent care credit?
per_question.response:
An employer-provided dependent care assistance program affects the child and dependent care credit in several important ways:

## 1. Must Complete Form 2441, Part III First
If you received any dependent care benefits from your employer during the year, you **must complete Form 2441, Part III** before you can figure the amount of your credit [p503, p.1-2]. This step is required to determine how much, if any, of the benefits can be excluded from your income.

## 2. Excluded Benefits Are Not Counted as Work-Related Expenses
If you exclude dependent care benefits from your income, the amount of the excluded benefits:
- **Is not included** in your work-related expenses used to calculate the credit; and
- **Reduces the dollar limit** on expenses you can use for the credit [p503, p.11].

## 3. The Dollar Limit Is Reduced
The maximum dollar limit on expenses eligible for the credit ($3,000 for one qualifying person; $6,000 for two or more) is reduced dollar-for-dollar by any dependent care benefits you exclude or deduct from income [p503, p.12].

**Example 1 (one child):** George has one qualifying child and the normal dollar limit is $3,000. His employer pays $1,000 directly to his dependent care provider, which George excludes from income. His reduced dollar limit becomes only $2,000 ($3,000 − $1,000), so he can only use $2,000 of his $2,900 in actual expenses to figure the credit [p503, p.12].

**Example 2 (two children):** Randall is married with two qualifying children (normal dollar limit: $6,000) and elected the maximum $5,000 pre-tax exclusion through his employer's dependent care flexible spending arrangement. His reduced dollar limit is only $1,000 ($6,000 − $5,000), so he figures his credit on just $1,000 of his $6,000 in work-related expenses [p503, pp.12-13].

**Example 3 (mixed expenses):** Roger and Megan had $19,500 in total dependent care expenses and received $1,000 in employer-provided benefits, which they excluded. Their dollar limit for two or more children was reduced from $6,000 to $5,000 ($6,000 − $1,000), and they figure their credit on the remaining $18,500 of expenses (subject to the $5,000 reduced limit) [p503, p.13].

## 4. Maximum Exclusion Amounts
The maximum amount of employer-provided dependent care benefits that can be excluded from income is **$5,000** (or **$2,500** if married filing separately). Any benefits exceeding this maximum will be included in your wages shown in box 1 of your Form W-2 [p503, p.11].

## Summary
In short, employer-provided dependent care benefits reduce — but do not eliminate — your ability to claim the child and dependent care credit. You can still claim the credit on any remaining eligible expenses after accounting for the excluded benefits, but you cannot "double-dip" by using the same expenses for both the exclusion and the credit [p503, pp.11-13].

per_question.user_input: What is the safe harbor rule for avoiding the underpayment penalty on estimated taxes?
per_question.response:
The safe harbor rule for avoiding the underpayment penalty on estimated taxes involves several conditions. You generally will **not** owe an underpayment penalty if **any one** of the following applies:

1. **Prior-Year Tax Safe Harbor**: The total of your withholding and estimated tax payments was at least as much as your prior-year tax — or **110% of your prior-year tax** if your AGI was more than **$150,000** ($75,000 if your 2025 filing status is married filing separately) — and you paid all required estimated tax payments on time [Pub 17, pp.46-47].

2. **90% of Current-Year Tax**: The tax balance due on your return is no more than **10% of your total current-year tax** (i.e., you paid at least 90% of your current-year tax), and you paid all required estimated tax payments on time [Pub 17, pp.46-47].

3. **Small Balance Due**: Your total current-year tax minus your withholding and refundable credits is **less than $1,000** [Pub 17, pp.46-47].

4. **No Prior-Year Tax Liability**: You had no tax liability for the prior year, and your prior tax year was 12 months [Pub 17, pp.47-48].

5. **No Withholding/Low Tax**: You had no withholding taxes and your current-year tax less any household employment taxes is less than $1,000 [Pub 17, pp.47-48].

---

**Special rule for higher-income taxpayers**: If your 2025 adjusted gross income was more than **$150,000** ($75,000 if married filing separately), you must pay the **smaller of 90% of your expected tax for 2026 or 110% of the tax shown on your 2025 return** to avoid an estimated tax penalty [Pub 17, p.39].

**Farmers and fishers** have a special lower threshold — they need only prepay **66⅔%** (rather than 90%) of their expected current-year tax [Pub 505, p.32].

The IRS will generally figure the penalty for you, but if you believe you can lower or eliminate it, you must complete **Form 2210** (or Form 2210-F for farmers/fishers) and attach it to your return [Pub 17, pp.47-48].

per_question.user_input: When are quarterly estimated tax payments due?
per_question.response:
Quarterly estimated tax payments are due on the following dates:

**Standard Payment Schedule:**

| Period | General Due Date | Tax Year 2026 Due Date |
|---|---|---|
| January 1 – March 31 | April 15 | April 15, 2026 |
| April 1 – May 31 | June 15 | June 15, 2026 |
| June 1 – August 31 | September 15 | September 15, 2026 |
| September 1 – December 31 | January 15 (next year) | January 15, 2027 |

[Pub 505, pp.24-25]

**Important Rules and Exceptions:**

1. **Saturday, Sunday, or Holiday Rule:** If a due date falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or legal holiday, the payment is on time if made on the next business day that isn't a Saturday, Sunday, or holiday. [Pub 505, pp.24-25]

2. **January Payment Exception:** You don't need to make the January 15 payment if you file your Form 1040 or 1040-SR by January 31 of the following year and pay all remaining tax owed at that time. [Pub 505, pp.24-25]

3. **Late-Starting Income:** If you don't have income subject to estimated tax until a later payment period, you must make your first payment by the due date for that period. [Pub 17, p.44]

4. **Fiscal-Year Taxpayers:** If your tax year does not start on January 1, your payment due dates are the 15th day of the 4th, 6th, and 9th months of your fiscal year, and the 15th day of the 1st month after the end of your fiscal year. [Pub 505, p.25]

5. **Farmers and Fishermen:** If at least two-thirds of your gross income is from farming or fishing, you have only one payment due date — January 15 of the following year. If you file your return by March 1 and pay all tax owed, no estimated tax payment is required at all. [Pub 505, p.25]

6. **Mailed Payments:** If a payment is mailed, the date of the U.S. postmark is generally considered the date of payment, though note that the postmarked date is the date processed at the postal facility, which may differ from when you dropped it off. [Pub 505, p.24]

per_question.user_input: How much tax must I expect to owe before I am required to make estimated tax payments?
per_question.response:
Generally, you are required to make estimated tax payments if **both** of the following conditions apply [Pub 505, pp.20-21]:

1. **You expect to owe at least $1,000 in tax for 2026** after subtracting your withholding and refundable tax credits (do not subtract any estimated tax payments already made). [Pub 505, pp.20-21]

2. **You expect your withholding and tax credits to be less than the smaller of:**
   - **90%** of the tax to be shown on your 2026 tax return, **or**
   - **100%** of the tax shown on your 2025 tax return (your 2025 return must cover all 12 months). [Pub 505, pp.20-21]

In other words, the key threshold is **$1,000**. If after subtracting your withholding and refundable credits your remaining tax bill is less than $1,000, you are **not** required to make estimated tax payments [Pub 505, pp.32-33].

**Special Rules:**
- **Farmers and fishers:** If at least two-thirds of your gross income is from farming or fishing, substitute **66⅔%** for the 90% figure in condition 2a above. [Pub 17, pp.42-43]
- **Higher-income taxpayers:** If your adjusted gross income (AGI) for 2025 was more than **$150,000** (or $75,000 if married filing separately), substitute **110%** for the 100% figure in condition 2b above. [Pub 17, pp.42-43]

**Exception — No estimated tax required at all** if all three of the following are true [Pub 505, pp.20-21]:
- You had **no tax liability** for 2025,
- You were a U.S. citizen or resident alien for the whole year, and
- Your 2025 tax year covered a 12-month period.

**Summary:** The primary threshold is **$1,000** — if you expect to owe less than $1,000 after withholding and credits, no estimated tax payments are required. If you expect to owe $1,000 or more, you must also check whether your withholding meets the 90%/100% safe harbor thresholds described above.

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum gain a single taxpayer can exclude from income when selling a main home?
per_question.response: A single taxpayer can exclude a maximum of **$250,000** of gain from income when selling their main home. This exclusion is increased to $500,000 for married couples filing jointly [p523, pp.2-3]. To qualify for this maximum exclusion, the taxpayer must meet the Eligibility Test, which includes requirements such as owning and living in the home for at least 2 of the last 5 years, not having claimed the exclusion on another home sale in the prior 2 years, and not being subject to certain disqualifications [p523, p.18]. Any gain above the $250,000 threshold would be taxable [p523, p.18].

per_question.user_input: How long must I have owned and lived in my home to qualify for the home sale gain exclusion?
per_question.response:
To qualify for the home sale gain exclusion, you must meet both an **ownership requirement** and a **residence requirement**:

1. **Ownership Requirement**: You must have owned the home for at least **24 months (2 years)** out of the last **5 years** leading up to the date of sale. For a married couple filing jointly, only one spouse needs to meet this requirement [p523, p.3].

2. **Residence Requirement**: You must have lived in the home as your primary residence for at least **24 months (730 days)** out of the last **5 years** leading up to the date of sale. The 24 months do not need to be consecutive — they can fall anywhere within the 5-year period and don't have to be a single block of time. Unlike the ownership requirement, **each spouse** must individually meet the residence requirement for a married couple filing jointly to get the full exclusion [p523, p.3].

**Exception for Disability**: If you become disabled, the residence requirement is reduced to just **1 year** (instead of 2 years) out of the last 5 years [p523, p.18].

**Key additional conditions** for the maximum exclusion ($250,000, or $500,000 if married filing jointly) include [p523, p.18]:
- You did not sell another home on which you claimed the exclusion within the **2 years** before the current sale.
- You did not acquire the property through a like-kind exchange in the past 5 years.
- You are not subject to the expatriate tax.

If you don't fully meet the 2-year ownership/residence tests, you may still qualify for a **partial exclusion** if the sale was due to a qualifying event such as a work-related move, health-related move, death, divorce, or other unusual circumstance [p523, p.18].

per_question.user_input: Do I need to report the sale of my main home on my tax return if my gain is below the exclusion limit?
per_question.response:
Generally, **no** — if your gain is below the exclusion limit and none of the special conditions apply, you do **not** need to report the sale of your main home on your tax return. Here is a detailed breakdown:

## When You Do NOT Need to Report

If **none** of the following three conditions are true, you don't need to report your home sale on your tax return [Pub 523, pp.20]:

1. You have taxable gain on your home sale and don't qualify to exclude all of the gain.
2. You received a **Form 1099-S** (Proceeds From Real Estate Transactions).
3. You wish to voluntarily report your gain as taxable even though some or all of it is eligible for exclusion.

So if your gain is fully covered by the exclusion limit and you did **not** receive a Form 1099-S, and you don't wish to voluntarily report, you can simply skip reporting the sale entirely [Pub 523, pp.20].

## When You DO Need to Report (Even If Gain Is Below the Exclusion Limit)

You **must** report the sale if **any** of these are true [Pub 523, pp.19-20]:

- **You received a Form 1099-S.** If you received this form, you must report the sale on **Form 8949** even if you have no taxable gain [Pub 523, p.20].
- **You have taxable gain** that exceeds your exclusion limit (e.g., more than $250,000, or $500,000 if married filing jointly) [Pub 523, pp.3, 8].
- **You choose to voluntarily report** the gain as taxable — for example, if you plan to sell another main home within the next 2 years and expect a larger gain from that future sale [Pub 523, p.20].

## Key Exclusion Limits

The maximum exclusion is **$250,000** (or **$500,000** if married filing jointly), provided you meet the Eligibility Test [Pub 523, p.3]. Only gain in excess of the exclusion limit is taxable [Pub 523, p.8].

## Summary

| Situation | Need to Report? |
|---|---|
| Gain below exclusion limit, no Form 1099-S received | **No** |
| Gain below exclusion limit, but Form 1099-S received | **Yes** (Form 8949) |
| Gain exceeds exclusion limit | **Yes** |
| Voluntarily choosing to report excludable gain | **Yes** |

If you voluntarily report and later change your mind, you can undo that choice by filing an **amended return within 3 years** of the due date of your return for the year of the sale (excluding extensions) [Pub 523, p.20].

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct a loss from selling my main home?
per_question.response:
No, you **cannot deduct a loss from selling your main home**.

According to IRS Publication 523, when you figure your gain or loss by subtracting your adjusted basis from the amount realized, if the result is a negative number (meaning your adjusted basis is greater than the amount realized), you have sold your home at a loss. The publication explicitly states:

> "If the number is negative (adjusted basis is greater than amount realized), you sold your home at a loss. **You can't deduct this loss**, but you don't need to pay any tax on the money you received from selling your home."

[Pub 523, p.16]

This rule applies to the sale of your personal main home. The loss is simply not deductible — but the silver lining is that you also owe no tax on the sale proceeds you received [Pub 523, pp.16-17].

**Note:** This is different from the portion of your home used for business or rental purposes. If you maintained a separate worksheet for business use of your home and that portion shows a loss, different rules apply and you would report it on Form 4797 — though that loss may be limited as well [Pub 523, pp.16-17].

per_question.user_input: Is unemployment compensation taxable income?
per_question.response:
Yes, unemployment compensation is fully taxable income. Here are the key details:

**Unemployment Compensation Is Taxable**
All unemployment compensation is taxable and must be included in your income [p505, p.12]. You must include in income all unemployment compensation you receive [p17, p.74].

**What Counts as Unemployment Compensation**
Unemployment compensation generally includes any amount received under an unemployment compensation law of the United States or of a state, including [p17, p.74]:
- Benefits paid by a state or the District of Columbia from the Federal Unemployment Trust Fund
- State unemployment insurance benefits
- Railroad unemployment compensation benefits
- Disability payments from a government program paid as a substitute for unemployment compensation

**How to Report It**
You should receive a **Form 1099-G** showing in Box 1 the total unemployment compensation paid to you. In most cases, you enter unemployment compensation on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 7** [p17, p.74]. If you did not receive Form 1099-G through the mail, you may need to access your state's website to get your electronic Form 1099-G [p17, p.68].

**Special Cases**
- **Private (nonunion) fund:** Unemployment benefit payments from a private fund to which you *voluntarily contribute* are taxable **only if** the amounts you receive are more than your total payments into the fund [p17, p.75].
- **Union payments:** Benefits paid to you as an unemployed union member from regular union dues are included in your income [p17, p.75].
- **Guaranteed annual wage:** Payments from your employer during unemployment under a union agreement guaranteeing full pay are taxable as **wages** [p17, p.75].

**Withholding and Estimated Tax**

per_question.user_input: Are workers' compensation benefits taxable?
per_question.response:
Generally, **workers' compensation benefits are not taxable**. Here is a detailed breakdown:

## General Rule: Tax-Exempt
Amounts you receive as workers' compensation for an occupational sickness or injury are **fully exempt from tax** if they are paid under a workers' compensation act or a statute in the nature of a workers' compensation act. This exemption also applies to your survivors [Pub 17, p.56; Pub 525, p.19].

## Key Exceptions and Special Situations

### 1. Retirement Plan Benefits
The exemption does **not** apply to retirement plan benefits you receive based on your age, length of service, or prior contributions to the plan — even if you retired because of an occupational sickness or injury. Those amounts remain taxable [Pub 17, p.56; Pub 525, p.19].

### 2. Workers' Compensation That Reduces Social Security Benefits
If part of your workers' compensation **reduces your Social Security or equivalent railroad retirement benefits**, that portion is considered Social Security (or equivalent railroad retirement) benefits and **may be taxable**. For more information, see Pub. 915 [Pub 17, p.56; Pub 525, p.19].

### 3. Return to Work
If you return to work after qualifying for workers' compensation, **salary payments you receive for performing light duties are taxable as wages** [Pub 17, p.56; Pub 525, p.19].

### 4. Disability Pensions with a Workers' Compensation Component
If your disability pension is paid under a statute that provides benefits only to employees with service-connected disabilities, **part of it may be workers' compensation and is exempt from tax**. The rest of your pension, based on years of service, is taxable as pension or annuity income. Similarly, if you die, the portion of your survivors' benefit that is a continuation of the workers' compensation is exempt from tax [Pub 525, p.19].

## Summary Table
| Situation | Taxable? |
|---|---|
| Standard workers' compensation benefits | ❌ Not taxable |
| Retirement plan benefits (age/service-based), even if retired due to injury | ✅ Taxable |
| Workers' comp that offsets Social Security benefits | ⚠️ May be taxable |
| Light-duty wages after returning to work | ✅ Taxable |
| Service-connected disability pension (workers' comp portion) | ❌ Not taxable |
| Service-connected disability pension (years-of-service portion) | ✅ Taxable |

per_question.user_input: What is the AGI limit for deducting cash contributions to public charities?
per_question.response:
The AGI limit for deducting cash contributions to public charities (also known as 50% limit organizations) is **60% of your Adjusted Gross Income (AGI)**.

Specifically, your deduction for cash contributions to these organizations is limited to 60% of your AGI, minus your deductions for all other contributions [p526, p.22]. This 60% limit applies only to **cash** contributions to 50% limit organizations (such as churches, temples, synagogues, and other public charities) — it does **not** apply to noncash charitable contributions [p526, p.24].

As a practical note, if your total contributions for the year are 20% or less of your AGI, none of these limits will affect you [p526, p.22].

Additionally, there is an important exception: a **30% limit** (not 60%) applies to cash contributions made **"for the use of"** a qualified organization (i.e., held in a legally enforceable trust for the organization), rather than contributions made directly **"to"** the organization [p526, p.24].

To calculate your deductible cash contribution, you multiply your AGI by 0.6, and the deductible amount is the smaller of your actual cash contributions or that 60% figure [p526, p.27].

per_question.user_input: What documentation is required for a charitable cash donation of $250 or more?
per_question.response:
For a charitable **cash donation of $250 or more**, you can only claim a deduction if you have a **contemporaneous written acknowledgment (CWA)** from the qualified organization, or certain payroll deduction records [Pub 526, p.30].

---

### 1. Contemporaneous Written Acknowledgment (CWA)

The acknowledgment must meet ALL of the following requirements [Pub 526, p.30]:

**Form:**
- It must be **written** [Pub 526, p.30].

**Content — it must include:**
- **a.** The **amount of cash** you contributed [Pub 526, p.30].
- **b.** Whether the qualified organization gave you any **goods or services** as a result of your contribution (other than certain token items and membership benefits) [Pub 526, p.30].
- **c.** A **description and good faith estimate of the value** of any goods or services provided. If the only benefit you received was an intangible religious benefit (such as admission to a religious ceremony), the acknowledgment must say so but does not need to estimate the value [Pub 526, p.30].

**Timing — it must be "contemporaneous," meaning you must receive it on or before the earlier of:**
- **a.** The date you file your return for the year you make the contribution, OR
- **b.** The due date, including extensions, for filing the return [Pub 526, p.30].

---

### 2. Multiple Contributions of $250 or More

If you made more than one contribution of $250 or more, you must have either:
- A **separate acknowledgment for each** contribution, OR
- **One acknowledgment** that lists each contribution, the date of each, and shows your total contributions [Pub 526, p.30].

---

### 3. How the $250 Threshold Is Calculated

Do **not** combine separate contributions when determining whether the $250 threshold is met. For example, if you gave $25 each week to your church, each weekly payment is treated as a separate contribution and does not need to be combined. Similarly, if contributions are made by **payroll deduction**, each paycheck deduction is treated as a separate contribution [Pub 526, p.30].

---

### 4. Special Rule: Payroll Deductions of $250 or More

If your employer withholds **$250 or more from a single paycheck**, you must keep [Pub 526, p.30]:
1. A **paystub, Form W-2, or other employer-furnished document** showing the amount withheld as a contribution; AND
2. A **pledge card or other document** prepared by or for the qualified organization stating the organization's name and that it does **not** provide goods or services in return for payroll deduction contributions.

If the paystub, Form W-2, or pledge card does **not** show the date of the contribution, you must also have another document that does show the date. If the date is already shown, no additional records are needed beyond (1) and (2) above [Pub 526, pp.30–31].

A single pledge card may cover all payroll deduction contributions regardless of amount, as long as it contains all required information [Pub 526, p.30].

---

In summary, the key requirement is obtaining a **written acknowledgment from the charity before you file your return**, containing the specific content described above.

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct the value of time I spend volunteering for a charitable organization?
per_question.response:
No, you **cannot** deduct the value of your time spent volunteering for a charitable organization. This is explicitly stated in IRS rules in multiple places:

1. **The value of your services is not deductible.** "You can't deduct the value of your time or services, including... the value of income lost while you work as an unpaid volunteer for a qualified organization." [p526, p.10]

2. **This applies even if a paid employee does the same work.** For example, if you volunteer 6 hours a week doing the same work as a paid receptionist earning $10/hour, you still cannot deduct $60/week for your time. [p526, pp.6-7]

3. **The value of your services is explicitly listed among contributions you cannot deduct.** "You can't deduct as a charitable contribution: ... 4. The value of your time or services." [p526, pp.8-9]

---

**However, you may be able to deduct certain *out-of-pocket expenses* incurred while volunteering**, as long as they are:
- Unreimbursed;
- Directly connected with the services;
- Expenses you had *only* because of the services you gave; and
- Not personal, living, or family expenses. [p526, p.7]

Examples of deductible out-of-pocket volunteer expenses include:
- **Transportation costs** (gas, oil, or a standard rate of **14 cents per mile**) to and from the place where you volunteer. [p526, p.7]
- **Uniforms** that are required, not suitable for everyday use, and worn while volunteering for a qualified organization. [p526, p.7]

Examples of expenses that are **not** deductible even while volunteering:
- **Childcare payments** made so you can volunteer. [p526, p.7]
- **Blood donations** to the American Red Cross or blood banks. [p526, p.10]

per_question.user_input: What form is required for noncash charitable contributions worth more than $500?
per_question.response:
For noncash charitable contributions worth more than $500, **Form 8283** is required. Specifically:

- **Total deduction over $500**: You must complete Form 8283 and attach it to your Form 1040. The IRS may disallow your deduction if it is more than $500 and you don't submit Form 8283 with your return [p526, p.33].

- **Deductions over $500 but not over $5,000**: You must complete **Form 8283, Section A**. This section is used to report noncash contributions for which you claimed a deduction of $5,000 or less per item (or group of similar items), as well as contributions of publicly traded securities [p526, pp.31-33].

- **Deductions over $5,000**: You must complete **Form 8283, Section B** for each item or group of similar items. In addition, you must obtain a qualified written appraisal from a qualified appraiser and have a contemporaneous written acknowledgment [p526, pp.32-33].

Your noncash contributions should be entered on **Schedule A (Form 1040), line 12** [p526, p.33].

per_question.user_input: What is the wash sale rule?
per_question.response:
## The Wash Sale Rule

### Basic Definition
A **wash sale** occurs when you sell or trade stock or securities at a loss and within **30 days before or after** the sale you [p550, pp.86]:

1. Buy substantially identical stock or securities,
2. Acquire substantially identical stock or securities in a fully taxable trade,
3. Acquire a contract or option to buy substantially identical stock or securities, or
4. Acquire substantially identical stock for your individual retirement arrangement (IRA) or Roth IRA.

More formally, a wash sale is defined as "a sale of stock or securities at a loss within 30 days before or after you buy or acquire in a fully taxable trade, or acquire a contract or option to buy, substantially identical stock or securities" [p550, pp.111-112].

### Key Rule: Loss Disallowed
**You cannot deduct losses** from sales or trades of stock or securities in a wash sale, unless the loss was incurred in the ordinary course of your business as a dealer in stock or securities [p550, p.86].

### Spousal and Corporate Attribution
If you sell stock and your **spouse** or a **corporation you control** buys substantially identical stock, you also have a wash sale [p550, p.86].

### What Happens to the Disallowed Loss?
If your loss was disallowed because of the wash sale rules, you **add the disallowed loss to the cost (basis) of the new stock or securities** (except when the acquisition is through an IRA or Roth IRA). This adjustment **postpones** the loss deduction until the disposition of the new stock or securities [p550, p.86].

### More or Less Stock Bought Than Sold
If the number of shares of substantially identical stock you buy within 30 days before or after the sale is either more or less than the number of shares you sold, you must match the shares bought with an equal number of shares sold (in the order they were bought) to determine which shares are subject to the wash sale rules [p550, p.87].

**Example:** You bought 100 shares of M stock for $5,000. You later bought 50 shares and then 25 shares of substantially identical stock. When you sold the original 100 shares at a $1,000 loss, you could not deduct $750 of the loss (on 75 shares) because you had bought 75 substantially identical shares within 30 days before the sale. You could only deduct the $250 loss on the remaining 25 shares [p550, p.87].

### Substantially Identical Securities
In determining whether stock or securities are substantially identical, you must consider all facts and circumstances. Ordinarily, stocks or securities of **one corporation are not substantially identical** to those of another corporation. Similarly, bonds or preferred stock are not ordinarily substantially identical to common stock of the same corporation — unless, for example, the preferred stock is convertible into common stock and meets certain other criteria [p550, p.87].

### Applicability to Options, Warrants, and Short Sales
- **Options and futures contracts:** The wash sale rules apply to losses from sales or trades of contracts and options to acquire or sell stock or securities. They do **not** apply to losses from commodity futures contracts and foreign currencies [p550, p.87].
- **Warrants:** The wash sale rules apply if you sell common stock at a loss and simultaneously buy warrants for common stock of the same corporation [p550, p.87].
- **Short sales:** The wash sale rules apply to a loss on a short sale if you sell, or enter into another short sale of, substantially identical stock or securities within 30 days before or after the short sale is complete [p550, p.87].

### Exceptions
- **Dealers** in stock or securities are exempt from the wash sale rules if the loss is from a transaction made in the ordinary course of business [p550, p.87].

### Reporting
Report a wash sale transaction in Part I or Part II of **Form 8949** with the appropriate box checked. Enter "W" in column (f) and enter the disallowed loss amount as a positive number in column (g) [p550, p.88].

per_question.user_input: How are qualified dividends taxed compared to ordinary dividends?
per_question.response:
Here is a comparison of how qualified dividends and ordinary dividends are taxed:

---

### Ordinary Dividends
Ordinary dividends are the most common type of distribution from a corporation or mutual fund. They are **paid out of earnings and profits and are ordinary income** to you — meaning they are not capital gains and are taxed at your regular income tax rates [p550, p.28].

---

### Qualified Dividends
Qualified dividends are a subset of ordinary dividends that receive **preferential tax treatment**. They are subject to the same **0%, 15%, or 20% maximum tax rate** that applies to net capital gain — significantly lower than ordinary income tax rates for most taxpayers [p550, p.28].

To calculate the tax on qualified dividends, you must complete the **Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet** in the Form 1040 instructions (or the Schedule D Tax Worksheet, whichever applies) [p550, p.34].

---

### Requirements for Qualified Dividend Treatment
To qualify for the lower tax rates, **all** of the following requirements must be met [p550, p.28]:

1. **Source:** The dividends must be paid by a **U.S. corporation or a qualified foreign corporation**.
2. **Type:** The dividends must not be of a type that is explicitly excluded from qualified dividend status.
3. **Holding Period:** You must have held the stock for **more than 60 days during the 121-day period** that begins 60 days before the ex-dividend date [p550, p.28].

For example, if you held stock for only 34 days of the required 121-day period, none of the dividends would qualify — even if reported as qualified dividends on Form 1099-DIV [p550, p.28].

---

### Additional Consideration: Investment Interest Deduction
If you claim a deduction for investment interest, you may have to **reduce the amount of your qualified dividends** eligible for the 0%, 15%, or 20% tax rate, by the qualified dividends you choose to include in investment income when calculating your investment interest deduction limit [p550, p.34].

---

**In summary:** Ordinary dividends are taxed as regular income at your marginal tax rate, while qualified dividends enjoy the same lower capital gains tax rates (0%, 15%, or 20%), provided the source, type, and holding period requirements are met.

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct investment interest expense on my tax return?
per_question.response:
Yes, you can deduct investment interest expense on your tax return, but there are several important rules and limitations to be aware of:

## What Is Investment Interest?

If you borrow money to buy property you hold for investment, the interest you pay is **investment interest** and is generally deductible [p550, p.45]. Investment property includes property that produces interest, dividends, annuities, or royalties not derived in the ordinary course of a trade or business [p550, pp.45-46].

## What Is NOT Deductible as Investment Interest?

- Interest incurred to produce **tax-exempt income** [p550, p.45]
- Interest expenses on **straddles** [p550, p.45]
- **Qualified home mortgage interest** [p550, pp.45-46]
- Interest taken into account in computing income or loss from a **passive activity** [p550, pp.45-46]

## Limit on the Deduction

Your deduction for investment interest expense is **limited to your net investment income** (investment income minus investment expenses other than interest expense) [p550, p.47]. Any disallowed investment interest can be **carried over** to the next tax year and treated as investment interest paid or accrued in that year [p550, p.47].

**Example:** If your net investment income is $6,800 and your investment interest expense is $8,000, your deductible investment interest is capped at $6,800, and the remaining $1,200 carries over to the next year [p550, p.48].

## When to Deduct

- **Cash method taxpayers** must actually *pay* the interest before deducting it [p550, p.46].
- **Accrual method taxpayers** can deduct interest over the period it accrues, regardless of when it is paid [p550, p.46].

## How to Report

- You must **itemize deductions** on **Schedule A (Form 1040)** and enter your deductible investment interest expense on **line 9** [p550, p.51].
- Use **Form 4952** to figure your deduction, and attach it to your return [p550, p.48].

### Exception to Filing Form 4952

You do **not** need to complete or attach Form 4952 if ALL of the following apply [p550, pp.48-49]:
1. Your investment income from interest and ordinary dividends (minus qualified dividends) is **more than** your investment interest expense.
2. You have **no other** deductible investment expenses.
3. You have **no carryover** of investment interest expense from the prior year.

If all three tests are met, you can deduct **all** of your investment interest expense [p550, pp.48-49].

per_question.user_input: What is the modified AGI phase-out range for contributing to a Roth IRA as a single filer in 2024?
per_question.response:
For **2024**, the modified AGI phase-out range for contributing to a Roth IRA as a **single filer** (or head of household, or married filing separately and did not live with your spouse at any time during the year) is:

- **Phase-out begins at:** $146,000
- **Phase-out ends (no contribution allowed) at:** $161,000

> **Note:** The excerpts provided primarily cover the **2025** limits (phase-out from $150,000 to $165,000) [p590a, pp.2] and reference that the 2025 limits are increases from 2024. Specifically, Publication 590-A notes the 2025 threshold of $150,000 is "up from" prior year amounts, and Table 2-1 confirms the 2025 single filer range of **at least $150,000 but less than $165,000** [p590a, pp.41-42]. The 2024 limits ($146,000–$161,000) are the standard figures from that tax year, but are **not explicitly stated** in the provided excerpts. The excerpts do not contain a direct statement of the 2024 single-filer Roth IRA phase-out range.

Based solely on what the provided excerpts contain, the **2025** modified AGI phase-out range for a single filer is **at least $150,000 but less than $165,000** [p590a, pp.41-42]. The excerpts do not provide sufficient information to confirm the exact 2024 figures directly.

per_question.user_input: Can I contribute to both a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA in the same tax year?
per_question.response:
Yes, you can contribute to both a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA in the same tax year. However, there are important rules and limits to keep in mind:

**Combined Contribution Limit**
Your contributions to both account types are subject to a shared annual limit. For 2025, the total you can contribute across all your IRAs (traditional and Roth combined) is:
- **$7,000**, or
- **$8,000** if you were age 50 or older by the end of 2025 [p590a, pp.5-6]

This means, for example, if you contribute $4,000 to a traditional IRA, you can only contribute up to $3,000 to a Roth IRA in the same year. The combined total cannot exceed the annual limit [p17, pp.79-80].

**Roth IRA Income Limits**
While there is no income limit for contributing to a traditional IRA, your ability to contribute to a Roth IRA may be reduced or eliminated depending on your modified adjusted gross income (AGI) and filing status. For example, if your filing status is married filing separately and you lived with your spouse at any time during the year, you cannot make a Roth IRA contribution if your modified AGI is $10,000 or more [p17, pp.79-80].

**Traditional IRA Deductibility**
Contributing to both types in the same year does not affect your ability to make contributions, but it may affect deductibility. Your traditional IRA contributions may or may not be deductible depending on your income, filing status, and whether you are covered by a retirement plan at work [p590a, pp.5-6].

**Key Takeaway**
You are free to split your annual IRA contribution between a traditional IRA and a Roth IRA in the same tax year, as long as your total contributions to both do not exceed the applicable annual limit ($7,000 or $8,000 if age 50+), and you meet the eligibility requirements for each account type [p17, pp.79-80] [p590a, pp.5-6].

per_question.user_input: At what age must I begin taking required minimum distributions from a traditional IRA?
per_question.response:
For **tax years 2023 and later**, you must begin taking required minimum distributions (RMDs) from your traditional IRA by **April 1 of the year following the year in which you reach age 73** — provided you reached age 72 after December 31, 2022 [p590b, pp.6-7].

Here is a summary of how the required beginning age has changed over time:

- **Age 73** – If you reach age 72 after December 31, 2022, you must begin receiving RMDs by April 1 of the year following the year you reach age 73 [p590b, pp.6-7].
- **Age 72** – If you reached age 70½ after December 31, 2019, but had not reached age 72 before January 1, 2023, you had to begin receiving RMDs by April 1 of the year following the year you reached age 72 [p590b, pp.6-7].
- **Age 70½** – If you reached age 70½ before January 1, 2020, you were required to begin receiving RMDs by April 1 of the year following the year you reached age 70½ [p590b, pp.6-7].

**Important notes:**
- Even if you voluntarily begin taking distributions before age 73, you must still begin calculating and receiving RMDs by your required beginning date [p590b, p.7].
- For any year *after* the year you reach age 73, RMDs must be made by **December 31** of that later year [p590b, p.7].
- If distributions are less than the required minimum, you may owe a **25% excise tax** on the amount not distributed as required (reduced to 10% if certain additional requirements are met) [p590b, p.30].

per_question.user_input: What is the additional tax penalty for taking an early distribution from a traditional IRA before age 59.5?
per_question.response:
If you take an early distribution from a traditional IRA before age 59½, you will face a **10% additional tax penalty** on the taxable amount of the distribution. Here are the key details:

1. **The 10% Additional Tax**: The penalty is 10% of the amount of the early distribution that you must include in your gross income. This is *in addition to* any regular income tax owed on that amount [Pub 590-B, pp.24-29].

2. **What It Applies To**: The 10% additional tax applies to the portion of the distribution included in gross income. It does **not** apply to any part of the distribution that represents a return of your nondeductible contributions (your basis) [Pub 590-B, p.29].

3. **Example**: A 35-year-old who takes a $3,000 distribution from a traditional IRA (with no nondeductible contributions) must include the full $3,000 in gross income and pay an additional tax of **$300** (10% × $3,000), on top of regular income tax [Pub 590-B, p.29].

4. **How to Report It**: Use **Form 5329** to calculate and report the additional tax [Pub 590-B, p.29].

5. **Exceptions Exist**: There are several exceptions to this rule — for example, distributions to a beneficiary after the account owner's death, or distributions to a terminally ill individual — where the 10% additional tax may not apply [Pub 590-B, pp.24-25].

6. **After Age 59½**: Once you reach age 59½, you can take distributions without being subject to the 10% additional tax [Pub 590-B, p.24].

per_question.user_input: What is the 60-day rollover rule for IRA distributions?
per_question.response:
Here is a comprehensive explanation of the 60-day rollover rule for IRA distributions:

## The Basic 60-Day Rule

You must generally make the rollover contribution by the **60th day after the day you receive the distribution** from your traditional IRA or your employer's plan [Pub 590-A, p.22]. For example, if you received an eligible rollover distribution from your traditional IRA on June 30, 2025, you must complete the rollover by August 29, 2025 (the 60th day following June 30) to avoid including the distribution in your income [Pub 590-A, p.22].

Any contribution made to your IRA **more than 60 days after the distribution is treated as a regular contribution, not a rollover contribution** [Pub 590-A, pp.23-24]. Amounts not rolled over within the 60-day period do not qualify for tax-free rollover treatment and must be treated as a taxable distribution — taxable in the year distributed, even if the 60-day period expires in the next year. You may also owe a **10% additional tax on early distributions** [Pub 590-A, p.23].

## IRA-to-IRA Rollovers

You can withdraw, tax free, all or part of the assets from one traditional IRA if you reinvest them within 60 days in the same or another traditional IRA. Because this is a rollover, you cannot deduct the amount reinvested [Pub 17, p.85].

### One-Rollover-Per-Year Limitation
Generally, if you make a tax-free rollover of any part of a distribution from a traditional IRA, you **cannot**, within a **1-year period**, make a tax-free rollover of any later distribution from that same IRA, nor from the IRA into which you made the rollover. The 1-year period begins on the date you **receive** the IRA distribution, not on the date you roll it over [Pub 17, p.85].

## Waivers of the 60-Day Requirement

The IRS may waive the 60-day requirement where the failure to do so would be **against equity or good conscience**, such as in the event of a casualty, a disaster, or another event beyond your reasonable control [Pub 590-A, p.22]. There are three ways to obtain a waiver:

1. **Automatic waiver** – You qualify if the financial institution receives the funds on your behalf before the end of the 60-day rollover period and you followed all procedures set by the financial institution for depositing the funds [Pub 590-A, pp.23-24].
2. **Self-certification** – You self-certify that you met the requirements of a waiver [Pub 590-A, pp.23-24].
3. **Private letter ruling** – You request and receive a private letter ruling granting a waiver [Pub 590-A, pp.23-24].

When evaluating a private letter ruling request, the IRS considers factors such as: errors made by the financial institution; whether you were unable to complete the rollover due to death, disability, hospitalization, incarceration, serious illness, restrictions imposed by a foreign country, or postal error; whether you used the distributed amount; and how much time has passed since the distribution [Pub 590-A, p.24].

**Important:** The IRS can waive **only** the 60-day rollover requirement — it cannot waive other requirements for a valid rollover, such as the IRA one-rollover-per-year rule [Pub 590-A, p.24].

### Amount Limitation for Waivers
The amount that can be deposited due to a waiver is subject to the same rules as amounts rolled over within the 60-day period. For example, if you received $6,000 from your IRA, the most you can deposit into an eligible retirement plan due to a waiver is $6,000 [Pub 590-A, p.24].

## Extension for Frozen Deposits

If an amount distributed to you from a traditional IRA or qualified employer retirement plan is a **frozen deposit** at any time during the 60-day period, two special rules extend the rollover period:
- The period during which the amount is a frozen deposit is **not counted** in the 60-day period.
- The 60-day period **cannot end earlier than 10 days** after the deposit is no longer frozen [Pub 590-A, p.24].

A frozen deposit is one that cannot be withdrawn from a financial institution because the institution is bankrupt or insolvent, or because the state restricts withdrawals due to financial institution insolvency [Pub 590-A, p.24].

## Plan Loan Offsets

For tax years beginning after December 31, 2017, if you have a **qualified plan loan offset**, you will have until the due date (including extensions) for your tax return for the tax year in which the offset occurred to complete the rollover — this is longer than the standard 60-day period [Pub 590-A, p.22].

per_question.user_input: Are qualified distributions from a Roth IRA tax-free?
per_question.response:
Yes, qualified distributions from a Roth IRA are tax-free, provided certain requirements are met.

**General Rule**
Qualified distributions from a Roth IRA are not included in your gross income. As stated in IRS publications: "if you satisfy the requirements, qualified distributions are tax free" [p17, p.90] and "You don't include in your gross income qualified distributions or distributions that are a return of your regular contributions from your Roth IRA(s)" [p590b, p.33].

**What Makes a Distribution "Qualified"?**
A qualified distribution must meet **both** of the following requirements [p590b, pp.33-34]:

1. **5-Year Rule:** It must be made after the 5-year period beginning with the first tax year for which a contribution was made to a Roth IRA set up for your benefit.

2. **One of the following conditions must also apply:**
   - Made **on or after the date you reach age 59½**,
   - Made because you are **disabled**,
   - Made to a **beneficiary or your estate after your death**, or
   - Used to pay **first-time homebuyer expenses** (up to a $10,000 lifetime limit) [p17, pp.93].

**Non-Qualified Distributions**
If a distribution does NOT meet the above requirements, it is not a qualified distribution. In that case, "the portion of the distribution allocable to earnings may be subject to tax and it may be subject to the 10% additional tax" [p590b, pp.34-35]. Additionally, unless an exception applies, "you must pay the 10% additional tax on the taxable part of any distributions that aren't qualified distributions" [p17, p.93].

**Summary:** As long as the 5-year holding period has been satisfied and one of the qualifying conditions (age 59½, disability, death, or first-time home purchase) is met, distributions from your Roth IRA are completely tax-free [p590b, pp.33-34].

per_question.response:
Based on the IRS Publication 596 excerpts, here is the information about the maximum Earned Income Credit (EIC) for a taxpayer with three or more qualifying children in 2024 (reported on 2025 returns):

**Income Limits (to be eligible):**
To claim the EIC with three or more qualifying children who have valid SSNs, your adjusted gross income (AGI) and earned income must each be less than:
- **$61,555** if you are single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse [p596, pp.4-5]
- **$68,675** if you are married filing jointly [p596, pp.4-5]

**Note on the Maximum Credit Amount:**
The excerpts provided do not explicitly state the maximum dollar amount of the EIC for taxpayers with three or more qualifying children in 2024. The EIC table excerpts included (pp. 38–41) only show partial credit amounts at higher income levels (where the credit is phasing out), not the peak/maximum credit amount [p596, pp.38-41].

The excerpts do confirm the AGI and earned income thresholds for eligibility [p596, pp.3-5], but the peak maximum credit amount for three or more qualifying children would be found in the full EIC table at lower income levels, which are not included in the provided excerpts.

If you need the exact maximum credit dollar amount, you would need to consult the full EIC table in IRS Publication 596 or the tax year's instruction booklet for Form 1040.

per_question.user_input: Can a taxpayer with no qualifying children claim the earned income credit?
per_question.response:
Yes, a taxpayer with no qualifying children **can** claim the Earned Income Credit (EIC), provided they meet all applicable rules.

**General Rule:**
IRS Publication 596 dedicates an entire chapter (Chapter 3) specifically to taxpayers without a qualifying child: *"Rules if You Do Not Have a Qualifying Child."* It states that if you don't have a qualifying child and have met all the rules in chapter 1, you must meet **four additional rules (Rules 11–14)** to qualify for the EIC without a qualifying child [p596, p.17].

Those four rules are:
- **Rule 11** – You must meet the age requirements
- **Rule 12** – You cannot be the dependent of another person
- **Rule 13** – You cannot be a qualifying child of another taxpayer
- **Rule 14** – You must have lived in the United States more than half of the year
[p596, p.1]

**Special Situations:**
Even a taxpayer who *has* a qualifying child may end up claiming the EIC without one. For example, if your child also qualifies as another person's qualifying child and the tiebreaker rules give that other person the right to claim the child, you cannot claim the EIC as a taxpayer *with* a qualifying child — but *"you may be able to claim the EIC without a qualifying child"* [p596, p.17].

This situation is illustrated in several examples:
- If you let your parent claim your child as a qualifying child for the EIC, *"you may be able to claim the earned income credit as a taxpayer without a qualifying child"* [p501, p.18].
- Similarly, if another parent has a higher AGI and claims the child under tiebreaker rules, *"you may be able to claim the earned income credit as a taxpayer without a qualifying child"* [p501, p.17].
- Likewise, in a scenario involving unmarried parents, *"you may be able to claim the earned income credit as a taxpayer without a qualifying child"* [p17, pp.34-35].

**Important Limitation:**
Not everyone qualifies. For instance, Publication 17 notes that a parent *"can't claim the earned income credit as a taxpayer without a qualifying child because your parent's AGI is more than $19,104"* — illustrating that income limits still apply even when claiming the EIC without a qualifying child [p17, p.35].

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum amount of investment income a taxpayer can have and still qualify for the earned income credit in 2024?
per_question.response:
For 2024 (returns prepared using 2025 Publication 596), the maximum amount of investment income a taxpayer can have and still qualify for the Earned Income Credit (EIC) is **$11,950**.

As stated under Rule 6: "You can't claim the EIC unless your investment income is $11,950 or less. If your investment income is more than $11,950, you can't claim the credit." [p596, pp.3, 7]

This limit is also confirmed in the summary of EIC rules: "Your investment income must be $11,950 or less." [p596, p.2]

Taxpayers can use Worksheet 1 to calculate their total investment income and compare it to this threshold [p596, p.7].

per_question.user_input: Can I deduct points paid when I took out a mortgage to purchase my main home?
per_question.response:
Yes, you may be able to deduct points paid when you took out a mortgage to purchase your main home. Here is a detailed breakdown:

**General Rule**
Points are a form of prepaid interest, and generally you cannot deduct the full amount of points in the year paid — they are typically deducted ratably (spread out) over the life of the mortgage [Pub 936, pp.7-8].

**Full Deduction in the Year Paid**
However, you *can* fully deduct points in the year paid if you meet **all** of the following tests [Pub 936, pp.7-8]:

1. Your loan is secured by your **main home** (the one you ordinarily live in most of the time).
2. Paying points is an **established business practice** in the area where the loan was made.
3. The points paid were **not more than** the points generally charged in that area.
4. You use the **cash method of accounting** (you report income when received and deduct expenses when paid — most individuals use this method).
5. The points were **not paid in place of** amounts ordinarily stated separately on the settlement statement (e.g., appraisal fees, inspection fees, title fees, attorney fees, property taxes).
6. The **funds you provided** at or before closing, plus any points the seller paid, were at least as much as the points charged. These funds can include a down payment, escrow deposit, earnest money, or other funds paid at or before closing — but cannot be funds borrowed from your lender or mortgage broker.
7. You used the loan to **buy or build your main home**.
8. The points were figured as a **percentage of the principal amount** of the mortgage.
9. The amount is **clearly shown on the settlement statement** (such as Form HUD-1) as points charged for the mortgage.

If you meet all of these tests, you can choose to either **fully deduct the points in the year paid** or deduct them over the life of the loan [Pub 936, p.8].

**What If You Provided Less Funds Than the Points Charged?**
If you meet all the tests except that the funds you provided were less than the points charged (test 6), you can still deduct points in the year paid — but only up to the amount of funds you provided. Any remaining points must be spread over the life of the mortgage [Pub 936, p.9].

*Example:* If you took out a $100,000 mortgage and were charged one point ($1,000), but only provided a $750 down payment, you can deduct $750 in the year paid and spread the remaining $250 over the life of the mortgage [Pub 936, p.9].

**Points Paid by the Seller**
If the seller paid points on your behalf to help you obtain your mortgage, you (the buyer) are treated as having paid those points. If all the tests above are met, you can deduct those seller-paid points in the year paid. However, you must reduce the basis of your home by the amount of seller-paid points [Pub 936, p.9].

**Important Distinctions**
- Points on a **second home** cannot be fully deducted in the year paid; they must be deducted over the life of the loan [Pub 936, p.8].
- Points paid to **refinance** a mortgage are generally not fully deductible in the year paid, even if the new mortgage is secured by your main home [Pub 936, p.8].
