per_question.user_input: Can I deduct interest on a home equity loan used to pay off credit card debt?
per_question.response:
**No, you generally cannot deduct interest on a home equity loan used to pay off credit card debt.**

Here's why:

The IRS is clear that interest on home equity loans is **only deductible if the borrowed funds are used to buy, build, or substantially improve** the home that secures the loan [Pub 936, p.2]. Using a home equity loan to pay off credit card debt does **not** qualify under this rule, since paying personal debt is not the same as buying, building, or substantially improving your home.

This rule is reinforced when reporting on your tax return: any interest shown on Form 1098 from a home equity loan "is not deductible if the proceeds were not used to buy, build, or substantially improve a qualified home" [Pub 936, p.10].

Additionally, to deduct any home mortgage interest at all, you must:
1. File Form 1040 or 1040-SR and **itemize deductions** on Schedule A.
2. Have the loan secured by a qualified home (your main home or second home) in which you have an ownership interest [Pub 936, p.2].

Even if those basic requirements are met, because the proceeds of the home equity loan were used to pay off credit card debt (a personal expense), the interest is treated as **personal interest, which is not deductible** [Pub 936, p.16].

**In summary:** The interest on a home equity loan used to pay off credit card debt is **not tax-deductible**, regardless of whether the loan is secured by your home.

per_question.user_input: What is the maximum American Opportunity Tax Credit per eligible student?
per_question.response:
The maximum American Opportunity Tax Credit is **$2,500 per eligible student** for 2025 [p970, p.10].

Here's how the credit is calculated [p970, p.19]:
1. **100%** of the first **$2,000** of qualified education expenses paid for the eligible student, **plus**
2. **25%** of the next **$2,000** of qualified education expenses paid for that student.

To claim the full $2,500, you must have paid at least **$4,000** of adjusted qualified education expenses for the eligible student [p970, p.19].

Additionally, **40% of the credit may be refundable** (up to $1,000), while the remaining 60% is nonrefundable [p970, p.10].

Note that the credit may be reduced or eliminated based on your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI): the phase-out begins at **$160,000 for married filing jointly** and **$80,000 for single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse** filers, with full phase-out at **$180,000** and **$90,000**, respectively [p970, p.10].

per_question.user_input: What is the modified AGI phase-out range for the American Opportunity Tax Credit for single filers?
per_question.response:
For single filers (as well as head of household and qualifying surviving spouse filers), the modified AGI (MAGI) phase-out range for the **American Opportunity Tax Credit** is **$80,000 to $90,000** [p970, p.20].

Specifically:
- The credit begins to phase out (gradually reduce) when MAGI exceeds **$80,000** [p970, p.20].
- The credit is **completely eliminated** when MAGI reaches **$90,000** or more [p970, p.20]; [p970, pp.9-10].

For comparison, married filing jointly filers have a phase-out range of $160,000 to $180,000 [p970, p.20].

per_question.user_input: How much student loan interest can I deduct per year?
per_question.response:
The maximum student loan interest deduction you can claim per year is **$2,500**. Here are the key details:

**Maximum Deduction**
Your student loan interest deduction is generally the smaller of:
- **$2,500**, or
- The actual interest you paid during the tax year
[p970, pp.33-34]

This deduction can reduce the amount of your income subject to tax by up to $2,500, and it is claimed as an **adjustment to income**, meaning you can claim it even if you don't itemize deductions on Schedule A (Form 1040) [p970, p.30].

**Income Phase-Out Limits (for 2025)**
The deduction may be reduced or eliminated based on your Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI):
- The deduction is **gradually reduced (phased out)** if your MAGI is between **$85,000 and $100,000** (or **$170,000 and $200,000** if filing a joint return).
- You **cannot claim the deduction at all** if your MAGI is **$100,000 or more** ($200,000 or more if filing jointly) [p970, p.34].

**Other Requirements**
To claim the deduction, you must meet all of the following [p970, p.33]:
- Your filing status is anything **except married filing separately**.
- No one else is claiming you as a dependent.
- You are **legally obligated** to pay interest on a qualified student loan.
- You actually **paid interest** on a qualified student loan.

**What Cannot Be Deducted**
You cannot deduct interest that was paid by your employer under an educational assistance program (for payments made after March 27, 2020), nor can you claim a double benefit for amounts already deducted elsewhere [p970, pp.33-34].

per_question.user_input: What is the Lifetime Learning Credit and how does it differ from the American Opportunity Credit?
per_question.response:
## The Lifetime Learning Credit and How It Differs from the American Opportunity Credit

### What Is the Lifetime Learning Credit?

The **Lifetime Learning Credit** is one of two tax credits available to help offset the costs of higher education by reducing the amount of income tax owed [p970, pp.21-22]. For the tax year, you may be able to claim a lifetime learning credit of **up to $2,000** for qualified education expenses paid for all eligible students [p970, pp.21-22].

A key feature is that **there is no limit on the number of years** the lifetime learning credit can be claimed for each student [p970, p.22].

**Refundability:** The lifetime learning credit is a **nonrefundable** credit. This means it can reduce your tax to zero, but if the credit is more than your tax, the excess will not be refunded to you [p970, p.22].

**Eligible students:** For the lifetime learning credit, an eligible student is simply one who is **enrolled in one or more courses** at an eligible educational institution — a much broader standard than the American Opportunity Credit [p970, p.76].

---

### Key Differences Between the Lifetime Learning Credit and the American Opportunity Credit

| Feature | Lifetime Learning Credit | American Opportunity Credit |
|---|---|---|
| **Maximum credit** | Up to $2,000 per tax return (for all students) | Up to $2,500 per eligible student [p970, pp.9-10] |
| **Year limit** | No limit on the number of years | No more than 4 tax years per student [p970, p.22] |
| **Refundability** | Nonrefundable | 40% may be refundable; the rest is nonrefundable [p970, pp.9-10] |
| **MAGI limit (2025)** | Same as American Opportunity Credit | $180,000 if married filing jointly; $90,000 if single, head of household, or qualifying surviving spouse [p970, pp.9-10] |
| **Student enrollment requirement** | Enrolled in one or more courses | Must meet stricter eligibility (e.g., first 4 years of higher education, at least half-time) [p970, p.76] |

---

### Choosing Between the Two Credits

- For **each student**, you can elect **only one** of the credits per year. For example, if you claim the lifetime learning credit for a child on your 2025 return, you cannot also claim the American Opportunity Credit for that same child in 2025 [p970, p.22].
- If you are eligible for **both** credits for the same student in the same year, you may choose either, but **not both** [p970, p.22].
- If you have the choice between the two, **the American Opportunity Credit will always be greater** than the lifetime learning credit [p970, pp.9-10].
- However, if you pay qualified education expenses for **more than one student** in the same year, you can claim the American Opportunity Credit for one student and the lifetime learning credit for another student in the same year [p970, p.22].

per_question.user_input: Are prizes and contest winnings taxable income?
per_question.response:
Yes, prizes and contest winnings are generally taxable income. Here is a detailed breakdown:

## General Rule
If you win a prize in a lucky number drawing, television or radio quiz program, beauty contest, or other event, you must include it in your income [p17, p.78]. For example, if you win a $50 prize in a photography contest, you must report this income on **Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i** [p525, p.35].

## Prizes in Goods or Services
Prizes and awards received in goods or services (rather than cash) must also be included in your income at their **fair market value (FMV)** [p525, p.35].

## Refusing a Prize
If you **refuse to accept a prize**, you do not have to include its value in your income [p17, p.78].

## Scholarship Prizes
Scholarship prizes won in a contest are not considered scholarships or fellowships if you are not required to use the prizes for educational purposes. You must include these amounts in your income on Schedule 1 (Form 1040), line 8i, **whether or not** you use the amounts for educational purposes [p525, pp.35-36].

## Employee Awards or Bonuses
Cash awards or bonuses given by your employer for good work or suggestions must generally be included in your income as wages. However, certain **noncash employee achievement awards** can be excluded from income [p525, p.35].

## Prize Points (Salespersons)
If you are a salesperson and receive prize points redeemable for merchandise awarded by a distributor or manufacturer, you must include their FMV in your income. The prize points are taxable in the year they are **paid or made available to you**, rather than the year you redeem them for merchandise [p525, p.35].

## Pulitzer, Nobel, and Similar Prizes
If you are awarded a prize for accomplishments in religious, charitable, scientific, artistic, educational, literary, or civic fields, you must generally include the value in your income. However, you may **exclude** the prize if ALL of the following conditions are met [p525, p.35]:
1. You were selected without any action on your part to enter the contest or proceeding.
2. You are not required to perform substantial future services as a condition for receiving the prize or award.
3. The prize or award is transferred by the payer **directly to a governmental unit or tax-exempt charitable organization** as designated by you [p525, p.35].

## Lottery and Raffle Winnings
Winnings from lotteries and raffles are gambling winnings and must be included in your income. This includes not just cash winnings, but also the **FMV of bonds, cars, houses, and other noncash prizes**. If you win a state lottery prize payable in installments, you must include the annual payments and any amounts designated as interest on unpaid installments in your gross income. If you sell future lottery payments for a lump sum, you must report the amount received as ordinary income in the year you receive it [p525, p.33].

Sharing/gig economy. A sharing economy is
one in which assets are shared between individ-
uals for a fee, usually through the Internet. For
example, you rent out your car when you don’t
need it, or you share your wi-fi account for a fee.
A gig economy is one in which a short-term

contract or freelance work is the norm, as op-
posed to a permanent job. For example, you
drive for a ride-sharing service, or work as a fit-
ness trainer, babysitter, or tutor.

Overtime. If you earned qualified overtime, you
may be eligible to deduct up to $12,500

overtime compensation. Your deduction will be
limited if your modified adjusted gross income is
more than $150,000 ($300,000 if married filing

Prizes and awards. If you win a prize in a
lucky number drawing, television or radio quiz
program, beauty contest, or other event, you
must include it in your income. For example, if
you win a $50 prize in a photography contest,
you must report this income on Schedule 1
(Form 1040), line 8i. If you refuse to accept a

prize, don’t include its value in your income.
Prizes and awards in goods or services
must be included in your income at their fair
market value.
Employee awards or bonuses. Cash
awards or bonuses given to you by your em-
ployer for good work or suggestions must gen-
erally be included in your income as wages.
